summary: Initial Layer 2A industry-chain map for the Energy theme, focused on Serenity-style chokepoints rather than obvious mega-cap leaders. The strongest mapped bottleneck clusters are: grid transmission/distribution physical hardware, utility procurement and approved-vendor gates, high-voltage power-quality/HVDC/FACTS equipment, transformers and switchgear, and nuclear fuel-cycle enrichment/HALEU. Low-attention value may hide in mandatory bill-of-materials suppliers, specification-embedded hardware, galvanizing/coatings, utility structures, electrical installation capacity, and nuclear fuel-cycle middle steps rather than only in generators, utilities, or large electrical OEMs.

supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Rising electricity demand from AI infrastructure, data centers, industrial reshoring, electrification, and renewables creates the upstream pull for generation, grid interconnection, transformers, switchgear, and transmission hardware. This is the demand origin, not necessarily the investable bottleneck itself.

supply_chain_map.node: Power generation capacity: gas, nuclear, renewables, storage
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Generation availability is the visible layer of the energy theme, but it can be constrained by interconnection queues, grid capacity, fuel availability, permitting, and equipment lead times. High-attention IPPs and utilities may dominate narratives, so this node should be used as demand context for upstream bottlenecks.

For nuclear and advanced reactor exposure, the uranium mine is not necessarily the scarce layer. Conversion, enrichment, HALEU production, licensing, fabrication, and domestic supply-chain reconstruction may be more binding, especially where policy seeks to reduce Russian supply dependence.

Uranium supply matters for nuclear fuel economics, but external context argues that global production capacity makes mining less likely to be the tightest near-term chokepoint than enrichment or HALEU. This node should be tracked but not allowed to crowd out mid-cycle fuel bottlenecks.

Mandatory, low-glamour hardware such as clamps, fittings, conductor supports, splices, motion-control devices, and line protection components can be specification-embedded. Utilities may be reluctant to switch suppliers because qualification, field reliability, and engineering standards matter.

Procurement decisions determine whether grid projects advance or stall before construction begins. Approved-vendor status, qualification cycles, supplier reliability, and utility engineering specifications can create chokepoints that are not obvious from headline capex numbers.

Transformers and related power-quality products are necessary for data centers, industrial electrification, microgrids, renewables, and utility distribution. Long lead times, capacity limits, and qualification requirements can shift economics toward suppliers with available capacity and established customer relationships.

supply_chain_map.node: High-voltage HVDC, FACTS, reactors, harmonic filters, and STATCOM
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Long-distance bulk power transfer, renewable integration, grid stability, and data-center power quality require specialized high-voltage equipment. Supplier qualification barriers, reliability standards, and limited global vendor pools may create bottleneck value in niche manufacturers rather than only large OEMs.

supply_chain_map.node: Switchgear, control gear, and engineered power distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Switchgear and engineered power-distribution systems sit between generation/grid assets and end-use load. Data centers, utilities, and industrial facilities may face lead-time constraints in this layer, but cyclicality and backlog quality must be verified.

supply_chain_map.node: Transmission and distribution structures: poles, towers, substations
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Grid expansion and hardening require physical structures such as steel poles, concrete poles, lattice structures, and substation structures. This is an adjacent, less obvious bottleneck where diversified infrastructure companies can hide utility exposure.

supply_chain_map.node: Hot-dip galvanizing, coatings, and corrosion protection
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Outdoor grid structures and steel components require corrosion protection. Galvanizing and coatings suppliers may benefit one step removed from transmission buildout, but energy exposure must be separated from general industrial activity.

supply_chain_map.node: Electrical conduit, raceway, cable management, and installation materials
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Data centers, substations, industrial facilities, and commercial electrification projects require large volumes of physical electrical installation products. This node may be dismissed as commodity construction materials even when it participates in power-infrastructure buildout.

supply_chain_map.node: Electrical contracting, field labor, and project execution capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even if equipment is available, grid and data-center power projects require skilled labor, electrical contractors, and execution capacity. Labor availability and project risk can become hidden constraints, but margin durability and customer concentration require verification.

Large contractors benefit visibly from grid and power capex backlogs, but they are higher-attention nodes. They are useful indicators of project volume and backlog conversion, while upstream suppliers may offer cleaner chokepoint exposure.

Utilities are the ultimate buyers and specification setters for much of the grid equipment stack. Their capex plans, procurement strategies, rate-base approvals, interconnection needs, and reliability standards determine which suppliers become embedded.

supply_chain_map.node: Hyperscalers and large industrial power buyers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Large buyers can accelerate demand for dedicated generation, nuclear contracts, power-quality equipment, substations, transformers, and transmission upgrades. Their announcements should be traced through actual interconnection, procurement, and supplier evidence rather than accepted as direct monetization.
